notes.meaning: God spoke to Moses and Aaron while they were still in Egypt, before the final plague fell. His words were given in Egypt rather than at Mount Sinai to show that Israel's journey with Him began right in the place of their slavery. The LORD addressed both brothers together because they were to lead the people together.

God reset Israel's calendar so that their whole year would now start with the month of their rescue. This spring month, later called Nisan or Abib, had previously been in the middle of their civil year. From now on, their religious life and calendar would begin with the memory of God setting them free.

differ.view: Israel was saved by God from God's own wrath, since as sinners they deserved judgment just like Egypt, so their new calendar marked a rebirth based purely on a substitute dying in their place.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The command did not replace the existing autumn civil new year, but designated this month as the first in religious enumeration to highlight the festival of freedom.

notes.meaning: Moses and Aaron were told to command every household in Israel to choose a lamb on the tenth day of the month. By bringing the lamb into their home four days before the meal, each family would get to know it and treat it as precious. The sacrifice was not just for the nation as a whole, but was centered in each individual family.

If a family was too small to eat an entire lamb by themselves, they were to invite their nearest neighbor to join them. The number of people was counted so that none of the sacred meal would go to waste. This rule encouraged neighborly kindness and made sure smaller households were fully included in worship.

The animal had to be a one-year-old male sheep or goat that was healthy and had no physical defects. Offering an animal in the prime of its life showed that God deserved their absolute best. Christians have always seen this pure lamb as a picture of Jesus Christ, who lived a completely sinless life.

The lamb was kept safe and watched closely until the fourteenth day of the month. At twilight on that evening, all the families across Israel were to kill their lambs at the same time. This shared moment united the whole congregation in one solemn act of worship and obedience.

The Israelites were told to take some of the lamb's blood and smear it on the top and two sides of their front doorframe. The blood was never placed on the threshold, so that no one would step on what was sacred to God. This mark publicly identified the home as one that trusted in God's mercy.

That same night, the family was to eat the meat roasted over a fire, along with flat bread made without yeast and bitter herbs. The bitter herbs reminded them of the bitter pain of their slavery in Egypt. Bread without yeast pointed to a life made pure and clean from sin, as well as the rush of their escape.

God commanded that the lamb be roasted whole over the fire, with its head, legs, and inner organs, rather than boiled in water or eaten raw. Roasting was the quickest way to prepare it for their sudden departure. Keeping the animal whole also prevented any of its bones from being broken.

None of the meat was to be saved for breakfast the next morning; any leftover parts had to be burned with fire before dawn. This rule kept the sacred offering from spoiling in the heat or being treated as ordinary food. It also taught the people to depend on God each day rather than hoarding food for the road.

The people were to eat the meal dressed for travel, wearing sandals on their feet and holding their walking sticks. They had to eat quickly because their deliverance was coming without warning. It was called the LORD's Passover because God was about to pass over their homes in mercy.

God warned that He would move across Egypt that night to strike down every firstborn son and firstborn male animal. By doing this, the LORD would also judge Egypt's idols and false gods, showing they had no power to protect their worshippers. He reminded them that He alone is the living God and ruler of the earth.

The blood on the doorposts served as an outward sign of God's promise to those inside. When the LORD saw the blood, He would pass over that house, and no deadly judgment would touch anyone within. Safety did not come from being good people, but from resting under the protection of the blood.

This night was to be remembered by Israel as an annual festival for all future generations. Celebrating it year after year would remind their children of God's great rescue and mercy. For Christians, this lasting celebration points ahead to the Lord's Supper, which remembers Christ's death until He returns.

For seven days following the Passover, the people were forbidden to eat any bread made with yeast, which is leaven. On the very first day, they had to search their homes and clear out all leaven entirely. Anyone who deliberately disobeyed and ate leavened bread was cut off from the religious community of Israel.

The first and seventh days of the week-long festival were set apart for special holy gatherings of worship. Regular daily work was forbidden on both days, treating them like a Sabbath. The only work allowed was preparing the food needed for each person's meals.

Israel was commanded to faithfully keep this Feast of Unleavened Bread because God brought their organized tribes out of Egypt on that very day. It was established as a permanent law so they would never forget how God delivered them. Looking back at past mercies helps believers trust God for what lies ahead.

The week of unleavened bread began on the evening of the fourteenth day of the month and ended on the evening of the twenty-first day. This set an exact seven-day period during which only flat, unleavened bread could be eaten. It linked the night of the Passover meal directly to the week-long feast that followed.

No leaven of any kind was allowed anywhere inside an Israelite house during the full seven days. This law applied equally to native-born Israelites and to resident foreigners who had joined the covenant. Anyone who broke this rule was separated from the fellowship and blessings of God's people.

God gave a final, sweeping command that no leavened food was to be touched in any of their dwellings. This made the festival a family practice that filled every corner of their daily home life. Keeping yeast out of their houses served as a visible picture of putting away sin from their lives.

Moses gathered the elders of Israel together to pass along God's instructions to the whole nation. He commanded each family to select their lamb and slaughter it for the Passover as God had directed. The leaders were expected to set the example so the rest of the people would follow in obedience.

The people were to take a bunch of hyssop, dip it into a basin holding the lamb's blood, and brush it onto the top and sides of their doorframe. Moses warned that no one was to step outside the doorway of their house until morning. True safety was found only inside the shelter of the sprinkled blood.

When the LORD passed through Egypt to bring judgment, He would see the blood on the doorframe and pass over that house. The destroying angel, acting as God's servant, would not be permitted to enter or harm anyone inside. It was the life given in the sacrifice that shielded the family from death.

Israel was ordered to keep this Passover service as an enduring law for themselves and all their descendants. Although putting blood on doorposts happened only on that first night in Egypt, the sacrifice and meal were to continue through history. God wanted future generations to know that His covenant promises remained true.

Even while they were still trapped in Egypt, God told them to keep this festival after they entered the Promised Land. This command gave them firm confidence that God would fulfill His ancient promise to Abraham. Remembering their rescue would keep their hearts grateful once they were settled and comfortable in Canaan.

God designed the unusual details of the Passover meal so that curious children would ask their parents what the service meant. These natural questions opened the door for parents to share the true story of God's power and mercy. Teaching children the meaning of God's works keeps living faith strong from one generation to the next.
